newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians find guerrilla escape tunnel at prison.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians find guerrilla escape tunnel at prison.

text.p: Peruvian police found a tunnel on Wednesday through which teenaged Marxist rebels planned to escape from jail while their comrades held 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home, the government said.
The discovery was announced only a few hours after the latest round of face-to-face negotiations between the government and rebels aimed at resolving the 86-day hostage crisis peacefully.
Last week the rebels called off talks amid accusations that the government was building a secret tunnel to storm the ambassador's residence and free the hostages.
Late on Wednesday, police discovered a 120 foot-(40 metre) long tunnel extending from a youth prison in the Lima neighbourhood of Maranga toward nearby buildings, said an Interior Ministry statement.

The tunnel was being built by jailed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrilla Leoncio Lopez Lazo "in the company of other convicted terrorists belonging to MRTA" and was nearly finished, it said.
"The massive escape was planned for Saturday, March 15, in the morning hours," said the statement.

It was unclear how many MRTA guerrillas were held in the prison, which is only for people under the age of 18 convicted of "terrorism" or common crimes, or whether they were among the roughly 450 rebels for whom MRTA leaders are demanding freedom in exchange for releasing the hostages.
The tunnel had ample electric lighting to allow the guerrillas to excavate during the night, the statement said.

Local television showed a hole in the street outside the prison leading down to what looked like a crudely dug tunnel. One radio broadcaster said two youths digging the tunnel were trapped inside when police made the discovery and were later rescued by police.

MRTA rebels have experience in digging their way out of prison. About 50 of them escaped from Peru's top security jail in 1990 through a tunnel, including some of the rebels currently holding hostages in the Japanese residence.
The timing of the discovery could hardly have come at a more delicate moment.
Talks to resolve the standoff at the ambassador's residence resumed on Wednesday after a tense, week-long hiatus in which first the guerrillas and then the government boycotted talks.
But the 10th round of talks on Wednesday -- between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa -- brought no sign of agreement, except to meet again at some unspecified date.

A statement from a three-member committee overseeing the talks noted that the meeting was held with "the same cordiality" as previous ones and had involved mutual discussion of each side's initial positions.
The statement hinted that both sides would need to loosen their positions for progress to be made.

"With there not being agreements on some matters, a stage of reflection is necessary, in which the guarantors' commission and the observer will seek to facilitate through separate meetings alternatives that make a solution viable," said the statement read by Peruvian Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, the Vatican's representative on the committee.
He said the committee, which also includes Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross chief representative Michel Minnig, would soon announce the date of an 11th round of talks.
Last Thursday, the rebels refused to attend talks, accusing the government of planning to take the building by storm through a secret tunnel.
The government then spurned a new meeting set for Monday, charging the rebels with trying to backtrack on the progress already made.
